analysis.one_liner: Caps the manufacturer price of insulin at $20 per 1,000 units nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in March 2023 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for insulin manufacturers to charge more than $20 per 1,000 units of insulin, whether sold in vials, pens, or cartridges. Insulin is a drug that millions of Americans need daily to survive, and its list prices have risen far above the cost of making it. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced in March 2023 and never received any further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 8 million Americans who use insulin — people with type 1 diabetes and many with type 2 — would gain if the bill passed, because the price manufacturers charge would be capped at $20 per 1,000 units. That cap would cover all forms of delivery, including vials and pens. People who pay out of pocket or have high-deductible plans would benefit most, since their costs track the list price most directly.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the price manufacturers may charge for insulin at $20 per 1,000 units, covering vials, pens, cartridges, and other delivery forms.
Applies to insulin licensed and marketed under the Public Health Service Act, which covers the insulin products sold in the United States.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers (chiefly the three companies that make nearly all US insulin) would bear the cost of the price cap if the bill passed, giving up revenue above the $20 ceiling. Middlemen in the drug supply chain — pharmacy benefit managers, wholesalers, and pharmacies — would not be directly capped and could keep their markups, which is why the bill addresses only part of the pricing chain.

drawbacks.text: A hard price cap could reduce manufacturers' returns on insulin, and drug makers argue this risks less investment in future insulin formulations and research; any supply disruption would fall hardest on the people who depend on the drug daily.

The cap applies only to the price manufacturers charge. It does not directly limit the markups taken by pharmacy benefit managers, wholesalers, and pharmacies, so some patients' out-of-pocket costs could remain higher than the capped manufacturer price.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and large: the roughly 8 million Americans who rely on insulin, a drug that has been off-patent for a century yet still sells at prices far above its cost of production, would pay dramatically less. The main cost is the risk that a hard price cap makes insulin-making less profitable at the margin, which manufacturers argue could slow investment in new formulations or complicate supply. That argument is strongest for future, next-generation insulins and weakest for the existing products that dominate today's market. The bill also has a design gap: it caps only the manufacturer price and does nothing about pharmacy benefit managers and other middlemen, so a determined Congress could have paired the cap with supply-chain reform for a stronger result.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never came out — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and then the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 9, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill would have limited the price charged by insulin manufacturers to $20 per 1,000 units, a level far below typical list prices for many insulin products.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers are better off: they kept charging uncapped prices for the entire two-year Congress because the bill never advanced. Middlemen like pharmacy benefit managers also kept their place in the supply chain.

for.name: Original cosponsors including Reps. Jayapal, Tlaib, Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, and Pressley
for.role: Members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 19 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and no majority was assembled to move the bill out of committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair Cathy McMorris Rodgers, R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 9, 2023 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
against.what_they_did: The three companies that make nearly all US insulin have long campaigned against price controls on their products and benefited from the bill never advancing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 19 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill received no committee action in a chamber where Republicans held the majority.

industries.note: The bill would cap what insulin makers can charge at $20 per 1,000 units, a fraction of the list prices insulin products have carried for years. Because the bill died, insulin makers kept charging uncapped prices for the full two-year Congress.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug supply-chain middlemen
industries.note: The cap targets only the manufacturer price, leaving the markups taken by pharmacy benefit managers, wholesalers, and pharmacies untouched. That makes the bill incomplete for patients, but it does not entrench these middlemen either.
A government-set price ceiling on a major drug category would have set a precedent other drug makers feared could spread. The bill's death left that precedent unmade.
